detail: While planning V0, nearly committed to building the automated retro loop (v1) before dogfooding it by hand on a real project — build ahead of validation. Corrected: Wizard-of-Oz the loop manually first, then automate only if it produces value.

On the Two Way Invoice Sync dogfood, init.md's emitter (phase 4) wrote CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md with byte-identical content (confirmed via diff -q). Duplication violates token-economy T1, and Claude Code reads ONLY CLAUDE.md while AGENTS.md is the cross-vendor standard. Fixed: AGENTS.md canonical + CLAUDE.md = one-line @AGENTS.md import.

Built the strict-path-guard hook using permissionDecision 'defer' from an unverified claude-code-guide answer. 'defer' is headless-only and wrong for an interactive passive warning (correct: exit 0 + additionalContext, no permissionDecision). Caught by the crossed adversarial review + a grounding pass. Lesson: ground every API claim against the docs before shipping code — even a claim from a sub-agent. voice V2 (verify before asserting) applies to sub-agent output too.

The build plan specified `claude -p --output-format stream-json` for the llm/ adapter without ever running it. Live probing found three errors: stream-json errors without --verbose; a naive invocation inherits the caller's whole ambient config (MCP servers, plugins, SessionStart hooks) costing 140,682 input tokens / $0.84 for a one-word answer versus ~11.4k / $0.03-0.08 hermetic — a 10x cost gap that would have silently destroyed the frugality thesis; and --bare, the obvious fix, forces ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and never reads OAuth, which would lose the subscription cost advantage. Validating risk #1 at Step 0 instead of at integration time was correct. Same class as sig-0003.

Using --system-prompt (replacing rather than appending) made the model leak raw tool-call markup (</parameter>, </invoke>) INTO a schema-valid string field. Native --json-schema validation passed on a payload that was unusable. Empirical proof that the LLM verdict contract needs contamination detection plus validate-and-retry, not just schema validation — the design assumed schema validation would be sufficient. Fixed in core/llm/verdict.ts with the real payload as a regression fixture; --append-system-prompt is now mandatory.

The first contamination check matched a bare ' is unclosed') and turned every front-end review into a retry loop that fails closed. Caught by writing the false-positive test before trusting the guard. Lesson: a guard against garbage needs a test proving it accepts the legitimate case, not only that it rejects the bad one.

ADR-0008's pre-registered kill criterion was measured at Step 0: a correctness lens returned 10/10 correct and unanimous on BOTH a known-good and a known-bad fixture (claude 2.1.225, sonnet, $0.79 for 20 calls). The agent-lens-can-earn-block assumption survives its first test. CAVEAT, recorded so it is not overclaimed: the fixtures are mirror-image and unambiguous (removing vs adding a null check before a dereference). This proves the harness works and the easy case is stable; it does NOT prove stability on borderline diffs, which is where a gate actually lives. Harder fixtures are owed before any lens ships as severity: block.

sig-0005's contamination rule rejected ANY tool-call markup in a verdict. Measured over 80 calibration runs, the artifact is a well-formed TRAILING suffix (the model closes its tool call inside the string) with complete, correct prose in front of it — and it is size-correlated: 0/40 runs on diffs under 10 lines, 13/40 on 11-15 line diffs. Rejecting the whole verdict discarded CORRECT answers and burned 3 billed retries into the same deterministic failure, leaving the gate blind on ~33% of realistic-length diffs. Fixed: strip the trailing artifact and report it via `sanitized`; markup embedded mid-content still fails closed. Re-measured live: 0/8 blind, down from 33%. Lesson: a guard written from a 2-sample observation was calibrated to the wrong failure shape — the rule was right in kind and wrong in degree.

`.sdd/architecture.md` recorded '--append-system-prompt clean 2/2' as evidence the contamination was fixed. That was 2 runs on a one-line prompt. At realistic diff lengths the same contamination recurs on a third of calls (sig-0008). The claim was not wrong so much as measured on an input unlike the real workload. Lesson: an evidence table is only as good as the representativeness of its inputs — record N and the input size next to any stability claim, not just the ratio.

`npm run calibrate -- --filter race` printed 'PASS — this lens may be declared severity: block' after measuring only 2 of 10 fixtures. A subset run that emits the global promotion verdict is how a lens gets promoted on the fixtures it happens to be good at — the precise result-fitting ADR-0008 pre-registers against. Fixed: a filtered run now prints PARTIAL and states it cannot promote. Lesson: any tool that can run on a subset must say so in its verdict, not only in its invocation.

Changing an agent-lens prompt from 'does this introduce a bug?' to 'name a concrete failing input under the change's stated contract, else pass' removed nearly all false positives (nullish-good 8/10 -> 5/5, boundary-good 7/10 -> 5/5) WITHOUT introducing false negatives (all five known-bad fixtures stayed 5/5). The obvious risk of raising the burden of proof for `fail` — starting to miss real bugs — did not materialise at N=5. Lesson: a flaky agent-lens is often a badly-specified one, not an unstable one; rewrite the lens before concluding the check cannot be calibrated. Still FAILS the bar: race-good flips 1/5.

scripts/calibrate.ts kept its own copy of the review lens with a comment saying 'must stay in sync with .sdd/checks/correctness.md'. That is a receipt-integrity hole: on drift you calibrate one prompt and ship another, and the check's recorded `calibration:` block vouches for text that never ran — a receipt that certifies the wrong artifact. Fixed: the harness now loads the lens through the check registry. Lesson: anything that produces a RECEIPT must read the artifact it certifies, never a copy of it. Same class as ADR-0006's warning that a version string is not identity.

A deterministic check runs through a shell, so a MISSING BINARY is not a spawn error — the shell starts fine and exits 127. Read naively that is a non-zero exit, i.e. a failing check, so one missing tool would have BLOCKED every change in the repo and blamed the change for it. The gate lane found this by running the gate on this repo and now maps 126/127 to `errored`, checked BEFORE the exit code because a broken run usually also reports non-zero. Verified with npm and claude off PATH: two block-severity checks fully broken, verdict pass, blocking empty, exit 2. Lesson: 'the tool failed' and 'the code failed' arrive on the same channel (exit status) and must be separated deliberately, or a gate blames the author for its own breakage.

While verifying the gate blocks on a real failure, the mutation I applied was a NO-OP: I pattern-matched `status: "renamed"` but the source has `status: letter === "R" ? "renamed" : "copied"`, so perl replaced nothing. The gate correctly returned pass, and I nearly recorded that as 'the gate fails to block'. Caught by checking whether the mutation actually landed AND whether the tests actually went red before trusting the gate's answer. Lesson: a negative test must first prove it broke what it claims to have broken — otherwise you are measuring your own patch, not the system.

The first `wst run` gated with --range HEAD, which means working-tree-vs-HEAD. The crewmate COMMITS its work, so by gate time the working tree is clean and the diff is EMPTY: the gate matched no files, applied no checks, and correctly reported 'nothing about this change was verified' — while `wst run` printed PASSED above it. The gate's honesty is the only reason this was caught; a gate that reported a bare 'pass' for an empty diff would have hidden it. Fixed: capture the base commit before dispatch and gate `base..HEAD`, plus refuse outright when the crewmate committed nothing. Lesson: 'no checks ran' and 'all checks passed' are different results and must never share a success message.

Diagnosing the above, I inspected the worktree AFTER the run had already released it. `treehouse return --force` resets the worktree to the pool base, so the tree I examined had no src/ and no package.json — and I announced the bug was 'far worse', that the crewmate had branched from the wrong commit and worked on an empty tree. Wrong: the branch ref survived, and it held exactly the right four-file commit. The evidence I was reading was destroyed by the cleanup I had just run. Lesson: when a run cleans up after itself, diagnose from the artifacts that SURVIVE cleanup (branch refs, logs) — and state which state you are looking at before drawing a conclusion from it.

The first real `wst retro` returned 3 of 4 proposals as the literal word 'placeholder', one explaining 'I don't have visibility into .sdd/skills/voice.md'. Cause: the proposer runs HERMETIC (no tools, no filesystem, by design — it is a judge), so it was asked to amend a rule whose text it had never been shown. Fixed by putting the target skill's current content and the list of real skills into the prompt; the second run produced 5 substantive proposals citing real signals. Lesson: a hermetic judge can only reason about what is IN the prompt — every artifact it must judge has to be passed in, and 'it has tools' is a property of crewmates, not of judges.

The anti-poisoning gate checked that a rationale was non-EMPTY but not that it was substantive, so proposals whose entire body was 'placeholder' passed validation and reached the human. The model had honestly signalled it could not do the job and the gate treated that as a valid proposal. Fixed: reject placeholder/TBD markers and rationales under 60 chars. Lesson: a validator that only checks for absence will forward a non-answer — 'the model said something' is not the same as 'the model answered'.
